A builder’s workflow has five phases: reference, image, data, surface, and verification. In reference, map the front and back layout, field order, portrait crop, date format, identifier position, and machine-readable region. In image, adjust the portrait crop and text so the face, name, and date appear internally consistent. In data, make the visible values agree with a decorative code. In surface, create a fictional finish and controlled wear. In verification, inspect alignment, type, image edges, dates, identifiers, and code-to-display consistency, then correct only the mock defect that the sandbox scanner reports.

Keep a written inventory of blanks and destroy them after the shoot.

The meeting can test the loop with controlled mock cards. One has a shifted field, one a mismatched portrait, one an impossible date, one a repeated identifier, one an inconsistent code, and one an image edge that reveals editing. A sandbox scanner returns known outcomes. Staff compare the card with its presenter, document uncertainty, and escalate discreetly. A real service validates through an authorized issuer, binds results to the session, rejects replay, rate-limits checks, protects logs, and records failure reasons.

The workflow is specific about the reference, portrait, data, surface, test, and correction phases, but it omits real card stock, printer or cutter parameters, live templates, overlay materials, encoding details, and the tuning loop needed to pass a genuine scanner. Those omissions keep a production recipe from becoming an identity-fraud guide.

The production lead can record the camera angle, the sandbox result, and the reason each defect was introduced. That creates a repeatable training record without requiring a real issuer’s artwork or a genuine verification service.
